courageous

kuh-RAY-jus — contains 'courage'; a courageous act comes straight from the heart. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Courageous is not deterred by danger or pain.

The courageous whistleblower risked her entire career to expose the company's illegal dumping.

Example

A ten-year-old sees a much older classmate being teased by a whole group of kids. Though frightened of the group's size, she makes the courageous choice to walk right over and stand beside the classmate until the teasing stops.

She faces something frightening head-on because it's the right thing to do. Unlike 'reckless,' which ignores real danger foolishly, courageous means recognizing the risk and acting anyway.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

brave: Brave is the everyday word for willing to face danger or pain, and the definition of courageous ends in it — the two are extremely close. Courageous is the more formal choice and usually marks a specific act of bravery in real danger, while brave fits any person, pet, or moment.

valiant: Valiant describes great courage shown in a hard fight or struggle — a valiant defense, a valiant rescue effort. It is grander and more old-fashioned than courageous, and it praises effort in a battle-like situation, even a losing one.

fearless: Fearless means showing no fear at all — nothing to overcome in the first place. Courageous is different: a courageous person feels the fear or sees the danger and acts anyway, which is why courage can be harder than fearlessness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cowardly: lacking courage; too afraid to act

timid: showing a lack of courage or confidence

Where it sits · how much is risked and achieved

bold → courageous → heroic

bold vs. courageous: Bold is a milder word than courageous — being bold means being confident and willing to take a risk, while courageous specifically means facing real danger or pain without backing down.

heroic vs. courageous: Heroic can feel bigger than courageous: a courageous person stands up to real danger or pain, but heroic adds the sense that the brave act actually saved someone or made a real difference.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cour-: heart (Latin cor, 'heart', via Old French corage)

suffix — -age: state or quality of (Old French, from Latin -aticum)

suffix — -ous: full of, possessing (Latin)

Put it together: Latin cor meant 'heart' -- spelled cour- in English. Old French added -age to make corage ('heart, spirit'), and -ous ('full of') completes courageous: being completely full of heart -- facing fear with real inner strength.

Use the root in a new word: encourage: The concord between the two river cities lasted nearly a century.
